opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "succeed."

If you mean building a robot that does one narrow task in a really structured environment, like picking a specific part off a conveyor belt in a factory, that technology has been ready for a while. People have built real businesses around that. The hard part there is less the AI and more the economics: integration costs, finding a use case where the robot beats a person or a fixed piece of automation, and dealing with the long tail of edge cases that show up once you actually deploy.

What I'm most excited about, and what I think is newly possible, is the more general-purpose direction. Systems that can take in camera images and maybe a language instruction and output actions, and that can handle a much broader range of tasks and environments. In the last couple of years we've seen real progress there. Models trained on lots of diverse robot data can fold laundry, clean up a kitchen, or bus a table in ways that were really hard to imagine five years ago. So the foundation is starting to form.

But I'd be cautious about saying it's "solved" or that you can just drop a robot into any home today and have it work reliably. Reliability is still the big gap. A demo that works 80% of the time is impressive in research, but for a product you often need something much closer to 99%-plus, and getting that last stretch is a lot of work. Generalizing to truly new environments, new objects, and new lighting is improving, but it's not where it needs to be for a lot of applications.

So the way I think about it: if you're starting a robotics company today, you want to be honest about where the technology actually is, pick applications where today's level of capability and reliability is enough to deliver value, and set yourself up to collect data and improve as the models improve. Data is still a huge bottleneck in robotics. We don't have an internet's worth of robot data the way language models have text. So companies that find a way to get robots deployed, even in somewhat constrained settings, and get that data flywheel going are going to be in a really strong position.

I'm optimistic. I think we're at a point where the trajectory is clearly there. But I also think there's a real risk of overhyping it, and the companies that succeed will be the ones that are clear-eyed about what works now versus what's still a research problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "ready." If the question is whether we have robots today that can walk into an arbitrary home and do an arbitrary task, no, we're not there yet. But I don't think that's actually the bar for a company to succeed.

What's changed in the last few years is that the paradigm has shifted. It used to be that you'd build a robot for one task, in one environment, and you'd hand-engineer a lot of it, and the moment anything changed you'd be back to square one. Now we're seeing that if you train a single model on a large, diverse set of robot data, you get something that actually generalizes to some degree. It can handle new objects, new scenes, sometimes new tasks with a little bit of extra data. That's a fundamentally different starting point. You're not solving robotics from scratch every time; you're fine-tuning or prompting a foundation model.

So the way I think about it is less "is the technology ready" as a binary, and more "where is the frontier of what's reliable enough, and does that overlap with something people will pay for." And I think it does, in a growing set of areas. Things like certain kinds of logistics, some manipulation tasks in semi-structured environments, tasks where a ninety-something percent success rate with occasional human intervention is already valuable. Those are real businesses today.

Where I'd be more cautious is anyone who's premised entirely on the general-purpose home robot being here in eighteen months. There are still hard problems: robustness in the long tail, dexterity, the fact that we just don't have anything like the volume of data we have for language and vision. Collecting robot data is slow and expensive, and the scaling story isn't as clean yet.

But I'd also say this: the field has been surprised on the upside repeatedly in the last few years. Things that I would have told you were five years away in 2021 are happening now. So I think the right posture for a company is to pick something where today's capabilities are already useful, build the data flywheel around that, and be positioned so that as the models keep improving, you ride that wave rather than having to rebuild. The companies that treat data and generalization as the core asset, rather than a specific mechanism or a specific task, are the ones I'm most optimistic about.

r001.rationale: The response describes a recent shift to training large models on diverse robot data, improving generalization and making robotics more viable for some businesses today.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’re asking the robot to do. If you’re starting a company around a fairly specific task, in an environment where you have some control, the technology can be ready. If your business depends on a robot walking into any home and doing whatever someone asks, there are still substantial technical problems to solve.

One of the biggest gaps is between getting a robot to do something in a demo and getting it to do that thing reliably over and over again. You have to think about what happens when an object is somewhere unexpected, when the lighting changes, or when the robot makes a mistake. Can it recover? Does a person have to intervene? Those questions really matter for whether the economics work.

So I would look for a useful initial application where the robot can deliver value with its current capabilities, and where deploying it creates an opportunity to collect data and improve. You want a path to broader capabilities, but you also want the first product to be useful before you’ve solved all of robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by succeed. If you mean building a robot that can do anything a person can do, in any environment, I don’t think the technology is there yet. But if you mean building a company around a useful set of tasks, where you can deliver value today and expand what the robot can do over time, I think there’s a real opportunity.

One of the big questions is how you get that improvement loop going. Can you deploy something that’s useful enough that people want it, collect data from those deployments, and use that data to make the system more capable? In robotics, that’s harder than in software because collecting data involves physical hardware, and failures can be expensive.

So I’d look less at whether a company has a really impressive demo and more at whether it has a task it can perform reliably, an economic reason for someone to buy it, and a path to improving through deployment. You don’t need to solve all of robotics to have a successful robotics company.
